description: Day 1 Stream 2 talks from BSides Las Vegas 2021.

talks.title: How I hacked a bank using pen & paper
talks.teaser: Shows how a one-page paper power-of-attorney form gave outsiders access to a Norwegian bank account.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how Norwegian banks let one customer hand power of attorney over an account to someone else. Online this is tied to BankID, but a one-page paper form remains for elderly, disabled or offline customers. The speaker studied the largest Norwegian bank's version of that form and the information it relies on.

The required details turned out to be largely public. National ID numbers follow a predictable pattern based on birth date and a gender digit, so candidates can be generated and checked against a lookup service with no rate limiting. The bank account number is also exposed through ordinary activity, such as sending a parcel that requires cash on delivery. A phone call to customer service was part of the test, and the completed form, filled in with mixed pens and witnesses who did not grasp their role, was accepted. The account owner was never notified, and the granted access covered ten years of payment history, had a hard-coded expiry date and offered no granular limits.

Disclosure took months, with the bank and the financial supervisory authority informed before the story went public in March 2021. The bank moved to a two-page form requiring more documentation, and the researchers planned to test whether the new version could still be abused. The practical lessons are to treat national ID numbers as identifiers rather than secrets, to notify account holders when access is granted, and to build granular, time-limited delegation with clear logs. The talk also points to ISO 29147 and ISO 30111 as references for vulnerability disclosure and handling.

talks.title: Human Security Spaghetti & the Wall you're Throwing it at
talks.teaser: Shows how behavior-change techniques lowered credential capture and raised password manager adoption at a large organization.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the gap between knowing what to do and actually changing behavior. Using a personal weight-loss example, the speaker walks through a six-stage model of change and argues that raising awareness covers only a small part of the work. Treating awareness as most of the job, the speaker says, overlooks the sustained effort that lasting change requires.

The middle section describes a behavioral engineering program aimed at credential capture, a technique red teams rely on heavily. Working with the red and blue teams, the team chose a concrete goal: employees should report emails that send them to login pages. The blue team agreed that more reports were worth the extra noise, and comms teams added an anti-phishing footer for verification. On the technology side, the team used email filtering, external tagging and a corporate password manager whose autofill would fail on spoofed domains. On the human side, per-organization dashboards created passive and active competition, a "knighthood" with swag rewarded top performers, executives sent monthly messages, and Slack nudges reminded people when they typed risky words.

Over two years the reported results were a halved credential capture rate, a tenfold drop in susceptibility, more than doubled reporting and a tripled password manager adoption rate. The takeaways were to research the audience, partner with teams that already run behavior programs, point out behaviors as early as possible and adopt a password manager. In the Q&A, the speaker said that two-factor adoption would be the next focus.

talks.title: Secure Mail Takes Professionalism
talks.teaser: Compares major and privacy-focused email providers on jurisdiction, security features, legal resilience and price.
talks.summary:
Jeremy Brown opens with the problem of choosing a new email host when a mailbox underpins so much of a person's digital life. He wanted to judge operational competence, meaning infrastructure quality and mature processes, but found little public evidence of it. He therefore measured proxies instead: legal jurisdiction, security-related features, security-adjacent features, legal resilience, and price. The providers compared were Google, Microsoft, Proton Mail, Tutanota, Hushmail, and self-hosting.

In the middle section, he explains that data stored in the United States can be reached under the CLOUD Act, while Switzerland, Germany and Canada bring different privacy regimes. Google and Microsoft scored strongly on two-factor options and account recovery, and Microsoft's add-on scanning and cloud office tools stood out. The privacy-focused providers offered more basic 2FA, fewer aliases, and little visible evidence of court challenges. Hushmail's past disclosure case still shaped its reputation. Self-hosting moves legal exposure onto the operator, and he argued that the real time and hardware costs often exceed a commercial plan.

He concludes that features are weaker signals than operational competence, and that the size of a dedicated security team may be the best available indicator. In the Q&A he discussed how encryption limits full-text search and suggested that providers adopt password-authenticated key exchange and the DIME protocol.

talks.title: Bad Neighborhoods – data-driven detection of malicious internet infrastructure
talks.teaser: Presents a data-driven approach to detecting malicious internet infrastructure.

talks.title: Do You Understand the Words That Are Coming Out of My Mouth
talks.teaser: Outlines the main healthcare security risks, from phishing and ransomware to cloud misconfigurations and connected medical devices.
talks.summary:
Che' Jackson's Proving Ground talk at BSides Las Vegas examines the top security vulnerabilities facing healthcare organizations during the COVID-19 surge. The opening lays out the stakes: disrupted operations, ransomware recovery costs, harm to patient care, exposed records, and lost trust. Employees are presented as the first weak point, with phishing, insider threats, and missing security education cited as common entry paths.

The middle section walks through concrete scenarios. Phishing emails posing as HR or IT, and personal email opened on work laptops, are shown as routes for malware. Small practices are described as easy targets. Cloud misconfigurations are tied to HIPAA Security Rule risk-management duties, and multi-factor authentication, least-privilege access, inventory management, and layered defenses are proposed as safeguards. Connected medical devices, such as insulin pumps, are presented as a patient-safety concern, with network segmentation and tracking of patches and unsupported operating systems recommended.

The closing pushes for framing security in business terms, tying each risk to organizational goals and scaling controls to organization size. The Q&A covered segmenting medical devices from IT, the gap between news of attacks and executive action, and vendor compliance claims. The takeaway: compliance alone is not security, and someone must own the work.

talks.title: Gamification of Tabletop Exercises
talks.teaser: Shows how tabletop role-playing techniques can make incident response exercises more engaging and memorable.
talks.summary:
Kelly Ohlert, a longtime tabletop role-player and scenario designer, opens by contrasting standard tabletop exercises with tabletop games. Exercises, as government bodies describe them, are discussion sessions that test incident response and continuity plans, often driven by regulatory checklists. She argues that these sessions tend to be dull, stressful and forgettable, and that game design can help lessons stick.

The middle of the talk walks through a sample scenario about a fictional cat-photo startup with a small security team, a limited budget and a consensus-based spending rule. Players receive character classes that differ from their day-job roles, so legal, executives and engineers see each other's perspective. Ohlert then covers three recurring problems: teams that rarely meet, one dominant participant who holds all the institutional knowledge, and a room that is half asleep. Her fixes include special player abilities, removing a talkative player through an in-game event, and opening with a catastrophic regional outage to wake people up.

She closes by encouraging facilitators to treat exercises as an evolving journey rather than a static check, and points to existing tabletop gaming resources for incident response practice. The practical takeaway is that inexpensive, creative scenario design can expose coverage gaps, improve cross-team understanding and produce clearer evidence of lessons learned for auditors.

talks.title: GCP BigQuery as Security Detection Platform
talks.teaser: Shows how a serverless Google Cloud framework turns BigQuery log queries into scheduled security detections.
talks.summary:
The speakers, from the game studio King, open with the problem of storing and querying high-volume telemetry. The on-premise platforms they used were costly, hard to maintain, and slow or congested when analysts needed them most. They argue that Google Cloud's BigQuery, a managed warehouse that runs SQL over very large datasets, can also serve as a detection source, starting with Cloud Audit Logs such as admin activity and data access records.

Norberto García Marín then walks through the framework design. Each detection is a template holding an identifier, MITRE technique and tactic, category, severity, a description and a SQL query. Scheduler templates select groups of detections by metadata and set how often they run. Cloud Storage, Cloud Functions, Cloud Scheduler and Pub/Sub handle ingestion, orchestration and result publishing, while Terraform and Atlantis deploy changes from GitHub pull requests. Cloud Monitoring raises alerts when a function fails, and results are emitted as JSON messages for downstream tools. A sample SQL injection detection illustrates the output format.

The talk closes with planned work: an anomaly detection layer built from log data, using BigQuery ML clustering or Vertex AI, with Dataflow handling streaming feature extraction. Diana Kramer shares lessons on the learning curve of using a general data platform for security, and advises teams to start from tools they already use and to consult internal BigQuery experts. The main takeaway is that managed cloud services can be assembled into a detection pipeline that scales without heavy operational work.

talks.title: Analyzing AutoIt Malware: Tools and Techniques
talks.teaser: Walks through decompiling, de-obfuscating and triaging AutoIt-compiled malware, using a real-world RAT sample as a case study.
talks.summary:
Chris Neal, a threat researcher at Talos, introduces AutoIt, a Windows scripting language that malware authors favor because it is easy to write, can call functions in Windows DLLs and reaches COM objects. He explains that compiled AutoIt executables store a tokenized, compressed and encrypted script, and that decompilers can recover it. He compares the two common decompilers, prefers the one that handles obfuscation and altered start addresses, and notes that older tooling struggles with 64-bit binaries.

The middle of the talk works through a RAT family sample active since 2017. The presenter confirms it is a compiled AutoIt binary from its version metadata, decompiles it, and then deals with the two main obfuscation styles: execution-flow obfuscation and string obfuscation. For the string case he renames variables in the decoding routine, reimplements it in Python, and applies it to every call site using a regex. He also describes a faster but riskier method of instrumenting the script in the AutoIt editor, and advises disconnecting the analysis VM from the network before running anything.

The closing section covers what to look for once the script is readable: built-in macros used for system enumeration, functions that touch DLLs, the registry or the network, and COM calls through the object-get function. Embedded binaries stored as strings, including a helper DLL and a SQLite library used for a WMI query that lists installed antivirus products, can reveal further behavior. The Q&A touched on sample volume, 32- versus 64-bit handling and how AutoIt compares with PowerShell.

talks.title: Revisiting the Analog Hole: Using OCR and other techniques to exfiltrate data
talks.teaser: Shows how OCR and camera capture can pull sensitive on-screen data out of an environment without digital traces.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether optical character recognition can be used to pull data out of an environment. The speaker's core point is that any information a person must read has to be shown in an analog form, such as a monitor, printed page or projected slide, so a phone camera can capture it. Remote work makes this harder to spot, and a company laptop may leave no log of the capture.

The walkthrough covers how OCR works: converting the image to black and white, correcting rotation and scale, segmenting characters, words or paragraphs, and then recognizing them with older template matching or newer neural models. Photos taken at an angle need perspective correction first. Cloud and office tools were tested on captured images. Clean, high-contrast text came through well, while inverted text, background noise and skew caused errors. Other routes covered include screenshots, HDMI capture, and accessibility interfaces that dump application text directly. Encoded data such as base64 is hard for OCR engines to read reliably.

For defenders, the speaker suggests showing each user only the data they need, giving different users slightly different content so a leak can be traced, using visible but unobtrusive watermarks, and deploying endpoint data-loss tools that keep activity logs. Watermarks can be lost once text is re-extracted, so cryptographically verifiable data is a sturdier control than anything visual. The closing takeaway is that OCR-based exfiltration is most useful for mid-sized leaks or when a remote desktop is the only access path.

talks.title: AI in a Minefield: Learning from Poisoned Data
talks.teaser: Shows how poisoned training data skews machine learning models and how threshold-based learning can limit the damage.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short survey of AI risks, including deepfakes, discrimination in automated decisions, and attacks on models themselves such as evasion and training data leakage. It then focuses on data poisoning, where an attacker slips crafted or mislabeled samples into training so a model learns the wrong behavior. Simple averaging examples show how one malicious input can carry outsized weight, and real cases include a 2018 attack on a Gmail spam filter.

The middle section turns to web application firewalls, which learn a baseline profile of API traffic from sources that cannot be fully trusted. Mitigations include filtering suspicious origins, capping how much any single IP, user agent, or time window can influence learning, and comparing successive models for drift. The speaker then presents a streaming-friendly method built on boolean facts: a value is learned only after it appears across enough distinct entities, so memory scales with the number of properties rather than the volume of data. The approach covers parameter types, character sets and numeric ranges, and extends to decision trees and ensembles.

The closing point is that no single fix eliminates data poisoning, but threshold-based learning can raise the cost for attackers and limit damage if tailored to each problem. Anyone building models on user-supplied data should treat that data as an attack surface.

talks.title: A Journey To Zero Trust
talks.teaser: Walks through one company's zero trust rollout, covering use cases, product categories, device health checks and deployment lessons.
talks.summary:
The speakers from Copart, a company with about 8,000 employees across 12 countries, start by noting that zero trust means different things to different organizations, so they first defined it for their own environment. Their baseline required corporate workstations to present a certificate with multi-factor authentication and pass a device health check covering antivirus, network security and encryption before reaching email and internal apps. They sorted their use cases into user-to-cloud, user-to-on-premises and machine-to-machine access.

They compared three product categories: network-based gateways that deploy quickly but handle device health poorly, endpoint gateways resembling a VPN that raise privacy and battery concerns, and agent-based designs that verify certificates and health at the application layer. They chose the agent approach because it fit their existing management tooling and allowed flexible health policies across Windows, macOS, Android and personal devices.

Their main lessons were to secure leadership buy-in, be transparent with legal and HR about the data being tracked, and enroll willing employees before skeptics. Enrollment initially took 12 to 15 steps and drove many support calls, so the team worked with product engineers to make workstation enrollment zero-touch, tied to the identity provider login, and cut mobile enrollment to two or three steps. The talk closed with plans to extend coverage to remote engineer access and machine-to-machine traffic.
